hook.text: Spin a rigged wheel showing 10 or 65. Then ask: what percentage of African countries are in the UN? Answers follow the wheel.

buildup.text: People who saw 10 guessed around 25%. Those who saw 65 guessed around 45%. A random number moved their estimate.

discovery.text: This is anchoring: the first number you encounter pulls your judgment toward it, even when irrelevant.

twist.text: Experts are anchored too. Experienced judges give harsher sentences after rolling higher dice.

climax.text: Retailers exploit anchoring constantly. The 'original price' sticker exists only to make the sale price feel good.

punchline.text: The first number wins—even when it's nonsense.

quiz.question: What is anchoring?
options: A first number biasing subsequent estimates

details.summary: Anchoring occurs when an initial number influences subsequent judgments, even if the anchor is irrelevant. Asking people if Gandhi died before or after age 144 produces higher age estimates than an anchor of 9. Anchors affect pricing, sentencing, negotiations, and everyday estimates.
details.whyItMatters: Anchoring is one of the most robust cognitive biases. It distorts professional judgments in law, finance, and medicine despite expertise and awareness.
takeaways: Initial numbers bias subsequent numerical estimates
Even obviously irrelevant anchors shift judgments
The effect persists across domains and expertise levels

faq.question: Why does anchoring work even with absurd numbers?
faq.answer: The brain uses the anchor as a starting point and adjusts insufficiently from it. Even when the anchor is clearly random, the adjustment process pulls the final estimate toward it. This insufficient adjustment happens automatically and resists conscious correction.

faq.question: How does anchoring affect real-world negotiations?
faq.answer: The first number in a negotiation becomes the anchor. Making the first offer gives you anchoring power because all subsequent discussion revolves around that number. Real estate listing prices, salary offers, and legal settlements are all influenced by whoever sets the initial anchor.
